title: Jobs weakened — but the bond market is still refusing to give equities the full relief

summary.changed: The U.S. September jobs report was materially weaker than expected: nonfarm payrolls rose by 29,000 versus a 90,000 consensus, and the probability of the Fed leaving rates unchanged in October rose to about 80%. Even so, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield resumed rising and ended Friday around 5.281%.
summary.missed: That is the key late-morning divergence: the market reduced the risk of an imminent Fed hike, but long-duration bonds are not signaling that structural pressure has disappeared. One plausible interpretation is that investors still demand a high premium for inflation, energy, fiscal deficits and debt supply — not only for the Fed policy rate.
summary.watch: U.S. cash markets are closed today. Before the new week opens, watch the OPEC+ decision, follow-up on the reported attack on an Aramco facility in Riyadh and the projectile strike on a tanker near Oman, and Monday's U.S. ISM services report — especially its prices component.

sections.heading: 1. The jobs report gave the Fed relief — not long-duration bonds
paragraphs: U.S. nonfarm payrolls increased by only 29,000 in September versus a 90,000 forecast. Prior months were revised lower and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%.

The initial market reaction was logical: investors reduced the probability of another October rate increase. Reuters reported that pricing moved to roughly an 80% probability that the Fed would keep rates unchanged, up from about 74% before the report.

But then came the more important signal: the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield, a key long-term cost of money that influences mortgages, corporate financing and equity valuations, resumed rising and ended around 5.281%. The two-year yield was around 4.827%. In other words, easier near-term Fed expectations were not enough to stop the bond selloff.

sections.heading: 2. Stocks rose — but the stock-bond divergence deserves caution
paragraphs: The S&P 500 rose 0.73% on Friday, the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.19% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.49%. Rate-sensitive equities benefited from the reduced probability of an October hike.

However, equities rose while Treasury yields moved higher again. That is a divergence — two markets responding differently to information that often affects both. If yields keep rising at the start of the week, equities will have to choose between continuing to ignore them or repricing the cost of capital.

TLT is an ETF holding U.S. Treasuries with maturities of 20 years or more, making it especially sensitive to changes in long-term yields. For the thesis, lower odds of a short-term rate hike are not enough; the key question is whether long yields begin a sustained decline.

sections.heading: 3. Oil closed weak on Friday — but the weekend restored the risk premium
paragraphs: Brent settled Friday at $102.25 a barrel and WTI at $91.11. Downward pressure followed a G7 agreement to coordinate the release of 100 million barrels of diesel and oil reserves through the International Energy Agency, beginning immediately and running over four months.

Two risk events followed the close: the Houthis said they attacked a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles and drones, and UKMTO reported that a crude tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile near Oman. Saudi authorities and Aramco had not immediately confirmed the Riyadh attack, so the Houthi claim must be separated from verified damage.

XLE is an ETF holding the largest energy companies in the S&P 500. If crude opens the week higher despite the reserve release, that would indicate the market is assigning more weight to physical supply risk than to government inventories.

sections.heading: 4. OPEC+ today: the quota headline matters less than actual production
paragraphs: OPEC+, the group of oil exporters and allies including Russia, is due to meet today. Sources speaking to Reuters before the meeting said the seven core producers were expected to keep November output targets unchanged; no final decision had been made when this brief was written.

The more important fact is that Gulf producers are still pumping materially below targets because of war-related disruptions. OPEC data cited by Reuters showed the seven producers at about 25 million barrels per day in August — roughly 5 million bpd below February's pre-war level.
Therefore, 'no change in the quota' is not necessarily bearish for oil. If actual capacity to restore barrels remains constrained, the official target alone does not increase physical supply.

sections.heading: 5. Nuclear and power: the Vistra report remains important, but it is a separate story
paragraphs: Vistra is a U.S. power producer that also operates six nuclear reactors at four stations. Reuters reported that the U.S. government is expected to lend it about $4.2 billion to increase output at at least three stations, with an official announcement expected Monday.

The move strengthens the thesis that existing power infrastructure is being upgraded to meet data-center demand, but there is still no official number for additional megawatts, timeline or fuel plan. That means the impact on uranium cannot yet be quantified.

URNM is an ETF of uranium miners and nuclear-fuel-chain companies. The positive signal would strengthen if the official announcement includes meaningful added output and a fuel plan that raises uranium consumption; it would weaken if most spending is equipment and maintenance with little change in fuel demand.

sections.heading: 6. Watchlist — what has to happen for the picture to change
bullets: Long Treasuries and TLT: positive if the 10-year yield begins falling despite services data and energy headlines; negative if it returns to the recent high around 5.34% or breaks above it.

U.S. equities: Friday's rally gains confirmation if stocks keep strengthening while yields stabilize or decline. If yields rise and stocks weaken, Friday's divergence closes in the negative direction.
Oil and XLE: positive if crude rises after the OPEC+ decision and the Saudi/Oman headlines; weaker if the G7 reserve release keeps Brent and WTI under pressure.
Vistra and URNM: wait for Monday's official announcement and the megawatt, timing and fuel details before drawing a quantitative conclusion.
Monday, October 5: the U.S. ISM Services PMI is released at 10:00 a.m. New York time. Beyond the headline index, the prices component will be especially important given pressure in the bond market.

market_map: Weaker-than-expected jobs growth → less pressure for an October Fed hike → equities rise.
But the 10-year yield rises to 5.281% → long-term pressure remains → TLT and equity multiples stay sensitive.
A 100-million-barrel G7 reserve release → pressure to reduce fuel and crude prices.
Reported Aramco attack + tanker strike near Oman + expected unchanged OPEC+ target → the energy risk premium can return.

Watch for official confirmation or damage assessment following the reported Riyadh Aramco incident and the tanker strike near Oman.

contrarian.consensus: A weak jobs report should ease the bond market and support equities because the Fed can pause rate hikes.
contrarian.why_right: If labor-market softness continues without another inflation acceleration, the Fed can wait and both short- and long-term yields may fall.
contrarian.why_wrong: Long-term bonds also price inflation, energy, fiscal deficits, debt supply and term premium. Friday already showed that long bonds can sell off even as the probability of a near-term rate hike falls.
falsifiers: The structural-pressure thesis weakens if the 10-year yield falls clearly and persistently after the ISM data and energy developments.
It strengthens if the yield returns to recent highs despite softer data and less hawkish Fed expectations.

bottom_line: There is no new U.S. market price this late morning, but Friday's close sent a clear message: the Fed is only part of the story. The labor market cooled, stocks rose, and long-duration bonds still sold off.

That makes the 10-year yield, the OPEC+ decision and the ISM services prices component the three most important variables for the week's open. If long yields do not calm down, easier near-term Fed expectations may be less bullish for equities than the headline suggests.

title: The weak jobs report lowered the odds of a hike — but long bonds were not convinced

summary.changed: The United States added only 29,000 jobs in September, versus the Reuters consensus of 90,000. August was revised to 133,000, unemployment rose to 4.2%, and average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% month over month and 3.0% year over year.
summary.missed: The weak report cut the probability of an October rate hike to about 22.7%, but Treasury yields still ended the day higher. That strengthens the possibility that pressure at the long end also reflects term premium, energy and debt supply — not only the next Fed meeting.
summary.watch: There is no regular U.S. trading today. At the start of the week, watch whether TLT can rise when the 10-year yield falls, whether oil stays above $100, and whether the sharp decline in Western Digital continues or stabilizes.

sections.heading: 1. The jobs report was weaker than expected — and prior months weakened too
paragraphs: Fact: nonfarm payrolls increased by only 29,000 in September, versus a forecast of 90,000. August was revised from 162,000 to 133,000, and July was revised from a gain of 21,000 to a decline of 10,000. Combined, July and August were revised down by 60,000 jobs.
Unemployment rose from 4.1% to 4.2%. Labor-force participation increased to 61.8%. Average hourly earnings rose 0.1% month over month and 3.0% year over year.

Interpretation: weak hiring, negative revisions and softer wage growth reduce the urgency of another rate hike in October. They still do not prove a recession. According to the BLS, employment changed little across most major industries, and unemployment has remained within a 4.1%–4.3% range since March.

sections.heading: 2. The bond market rejected the morning reaction
paragraphs: TLT is an iShares ETF holding U.S. Treasuries with maturities of 20 years or more, making it especially sensitive to long-term yields. Yields fell immediately after the report, but the move later reversed.
By the close, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield had risen about 4.7 basis points to 5.281%, and the 2-year yield had risen about 4 basis points to 4.827%. TLT fell 0.3% to $77.48.

Interpretation: a weak jobs report was enough to reduce the odds of an immediate hike, but not enough to lower long-term financing costs. That is evidence that inflation concerns, energy, debt supply and term premium still matter. It does not prove which factor dominated on a single day.

sections.heading: 3. Stocks treated bad news as good news — but breadth was not clean
paragraphs: The S&P 500 rose 0.73%, the Nasdaq gained 1.19%, the Dow Jones added 0.49%, and the small-cap Russell 2000 advanced 0.9%. A reasonable explanation is that investors focused on the lower risk of an October hike.
Gains were relatively broad by share count: advancers outnumbered decliners by 1.67 to 1 on the New York Stock Exchange and 1.34 to 1 on the Nasdaq.
However, the Nasdaq recorded 224 new 52-week lows versus 57 new highs. It is therefore fair to say trading improved, but too early to conclude that market breadth has undergone a full trend change.

sections.heading: 4. Energy remains a constraint on bonds — and the stress has shifted to refined products
paragraphs: Brent is the global crude-oil benchmark. It closed nearly unchanged at $102.25 a barrel. WTI, the U.S. benchmark, fell 1.9% to $91.11.

Europe agreed to release diesel inventories after discussions of a French proposal to release 50 million barrels of diesel and a parallel 50 million-barrel crude release by members of the International Energy Agency.

The key fact is that the acute shortage now lies more in refined products than in crude oil. If oil remains above $100 and diesel markets stay tight, a weak jobs report alone does not guarantee lower yields.

sections.heading: 5. Western Digital fell on supply fears — not on a proven change in demand
paragraphs: Western Digital (WDC) makes hard-disk drives used in data centers, among other applications. Its shares fell 10.2% on Friday to $415.29.
Reuters reported that the decline followed a Nikkei report that Toshiba plans to double production capacity for hard drives used in AI data centers by fiscal 2027. Seagate also fell about 10%.

Interpretation: the market priced in supply and competitive risk. An announcement about future production capacity does not prove that WDC's pricing or demand has already deteriorated. The invalidation condition is actual weakness in orders, pricing or margins — not the headline alone.

sections.heading: 6. Cross-asset picture and second-order ideas
bullets: XLE, an ETF holding the largest energy companies in the S&P 500, rose 0.2% even as WTI fell 1.9%. One day is not enough, but repeated relative strength could indicate that investors are looking beyond the daily oil move.

Micron Technology (MU), a maker of memory chips including HBM used with AI accelerators, fell 2.1% on Friday after rising the prior day on a better-than-expected revenue forecast and $32 billion of customer commitments. The next question is the quality of conversion into revenue and margins, not only the size of the commitments.

COPX, an ETF of copper miners, rose 3.0%. URNM, an ETF of uranium miners, gained 0.4%. IBIT, an ETF holding bitcoin, fell 0.5%. No verified fundamental change was found that alone explains these moves, so they remain monitoring signals rather than new catalysts.

Construction employment increased by 11,000, and nonresidential specialty trade contractors added 12,000. That is consistent with infrastructure activity, but the data do not isolate data centers and therefore are not direct proof of demand for electrical equipment or energy storage.

The test next week is therefore not only whether stocks rise. It is whether TLT and long-duration Treasuries can finally respond to weaker data. Without confirmation from bonds, the relief in Fed pricing remains partial.

title: Bonds remain the pressure point — and today's inflation data could change the direction

summary.changed: The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield remains around 5.23%, near a 19-year high, even after expectations for an October rate hike fell following softer labor data and Fed commentary.
summary.missed: The gap between elevated long-term yields and lower odds of an immediate Fed hike suggests the bond selloff is not only about the next meeting; term premium, debt supply and longer-run inflation risk are likely playing a larger role.
summary.watch: At 8:30 a.m. ET, the PCE price index and the third estimate of second-quarter GDP are due. Micron reports after the close — both events can quickly reset the pricing of rates, bonds and AI-linked equities.

sections.heading: 1. Long yields stay elevated even as the market trims the odds of an October hike
paragraphs: TLT is an iShares ETF that holds U.S. Treasuries with maturities of 20 years or more, making it especially sensitive to changes in long-term yields. The key story this morning is not simply that yields are high — it is that they remain high even after the market reduced the probability of another hike as soon as October.
Reuters reported the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield around 5.23%, after it reached roughly 5.293% on Tuesday, the highest since 2007. The 30-year yield touched about 5.6206%, the highest since 2002.

After comments from New York Fed President John Williams and softer labor data, markets shifted to pricing roughly a 47% chance of an October hike, versus about 70% a day earlier. Long yields staying near their highs despite that repricing is consistent with a larger role for term premium and longer-term financing concerns.

sections.heading: 2. The labor market softened a little — but it still does not look like a recession
paragraphs: U.S. job openings fell to 7.079 million in August, below the Reuters forecast of 7.225 million and down from an upwardly revised 7.335 million in July. That is a clear sign of softer labor demand.
At the same time, layoffs remained low: layoffs and discharges fell to 1.641 million, while the hiring rate edged up to 3.3%. The data therefore point to cooling, not a breakdown in the labor market.

Consumer confidence also fell sharply to 81.9 in September from 88.6 in August. Fewer openings and weaker confidence are exactly the type of combination that can eventually slow demand — but Friday's payroll report is still needed for confirmation.

sections.heading: 3. Oil remains expensive, but actual supply flows still argue against a full shortage scenario
paragraphs: Brent is the global benchmark for crude oil. It traded around $103.43 a barrel this morning, while WTI — the U.S. crude benchmark — was around $89.63.

Prices were supported after U.S. President Donald Trump denied that he was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran. At the same time, Middle Eastern crude exports rose to about 16.328 million barrels per day in September, the highest since the regional war began.

That means oil is still carrying a geopolitical risk premium, but actual barrel flows are moderating the extreme shortage scenario. For bonds, whether oil stays above $100 for an extended period matters more than a single day's move.

sections.heading: 4. The under-covered development: AI infrastructure financing is becoming part of the story
paragraphs: Reuters has highlighted rising credit-market concern around the financing of AI infrastructure. Large projects are using more debt and off-balance-sheet structures at a time when government bond yields themselves are elevated.

This is not evidence of a credit crisis or impending defaults. It does change the question investors need to ask: not only how strong AI demand is, but at what cost data centers are financed and who ultimately bears the risk if returns on capital fall short of expectations.

For suppliers of electrical equipment, transformers and cooling systems, physical demand can remain strong while project financing becomes the bottleneck. That is why demand for equipment and the pace at which projects convert into revenue must be analyzed separately.

sections.heading: 5. China's manufacturing returned to slight growth — positive for copper, but not yet a trend change
paragraphs: China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index rose to 50.1 in September from 49.8 in August, exactly matching the Reuters consensus. A reading above 50 indicates expansion.
That is a small but real improvement after two months of contraction. For copper and industrial equipment, China's move back above 50 is supportive.
It is not enough on its own to offset a strong dollar and high global yields. A sequence of readings above 50 would be more meaningful than a single month.

sections.heading: 6. Watchlist — what would change the theses
bullets: TLT, the ETF holding U.S. Treasuries with maturities of 20 years or more: the setup improves if the 10-year yield falls and holds below 5.15% and TLT reclaims the $79–$80 area. It weakens if yields retest Tuesday's highs.
XLE, the ETF holding the largest energy companies in the S&P 500: relative strength while oil falls would be more meaningful than gains driven only by a geopolitical headline.

Forgent Power Solutions (FPS), a maker of electrical equipment and transformers for data centers and the power grid: its investor-relations page shows no new company release since September 15 results. The thesis now depends on backlog conversion and on data-center projects securing power connections and financing.

Micron Technology (MU), a memory-chip maker including HBM used with AI accelerators: tonight's earnings are the key catalyst. Guidance, HBM demand, margins and capex matter more than simply beating last quarter's EPS estimate.

Brighthouse Financial (BHF), an insurer in an acquisition agreement with Aquarian Capital: no new deal update was found from company sources this morning, so the spread to the deal price still mainly reflects closing risk and time.

Uranium and energy storage: no sufficiently strong new fundamental development was found this morning to justify a broad thesis change; the high cost of capital remains the more important macro variable for now.

But long-term yields remain near multi-year highs → investors are demanding more compensation beyond the immediate Fed path.
Oil above $100 + heavy debt supply + more expensive AI financing → the cost of capital remains the core story even while headline equity indexes remain relatively resilient.

contrarian.why_right: That may be right if PCE stays hot, oil remains above $100 and the 10-year yield holds above roughly 5.20%–5.25%.
contrarian.why_wrong: It may be wrong if the softening in JOLTS and consumer confidence marks the start of a broader slowdown and a more patient Fed brings buyers back to Treasuries.
falsifiers: The bearish bond thesis weakens if the 10-year yield falls below 5.15% and stays there after the PCE release.
The bearish thesis strengthens if PCE surprises to the upside and yields break back above Tuesday's highs.

bottom_line: The message this morning is not simply 'yields are high.' What matters is that they remain high even after expectations for an immediate rate hike have declined.

If PCE is soft today and yields still fail to fall, that would strengthen the case that the problem has shifted from the near-term Fed path toward term premium, debt supply and long-term financing. If yields fall sharply, the market may simply have been waiting for an inflation print that gives investors a reason to buy bonds again.

title: The 10-Year Treasury Yield Hits a 19-Year High — and the Pressure Is Spreading to Credit
summary:
What changed: the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield traded above 5.27% this morning, its highest level since 2007. The long-term Treasury fund fell 0.88% to $78.62, while the major U.S. equity indexes declined between 0.7% and 0.9%.
What the market may be missing: the pressure is no longer confined to government bonds. High-yield credit spreads widened to nearly 3 percentage points over Treasuries, their widest level since April, and investment-grade credit has also begun to weaken. This is an early sign that high financing costs are moving from asset valuations into companies’ ability to raise debt.
What to watch today: U.S. job openings and consumer-confidence data at 10:00 a.m. ET. Strong readings could keep the 10-year yield above 5.25%; downside surprises could give bonds their first relief before tomorrow’s inflation data.

sections.heading: 1. The bearish long-term bond scenario was confirmed
sections.body:
TLT is an iShares exchange-traded fund that holds U.S. Treasury bonds with maturities of 20 years or more, making its price especially sensitive to changes in long-term yields. It fell 0.88% Monday to $78.62 after trading as low as $78.27. That is below the $79 threshold we identified yesterday as bearish confirmation.

The two-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to 4.937%, the 10-year to 5.251% and the 30-year to 5.570%. The 10-year yield traded above 5.27% this morning, a 19-year high. At the same time, the market-implied probability of another rate increase in October climbed to about 70%, versus less than 20% a month ago.

The fact is that long-term bonds broke below the level we identified. The interpretation is that the market is pricing a combination of expensive oil, a strong economy and heavy debt supply — not one isolated factor. The thesis improves only if the 10-year yield falls below 5.15% and TLT rises above $79.30; a drop below $78.25 alongside a yield above 5.25% would increase the risk.

sections.heading: 2. The equity decline was broad, but the fear gauge still does not signal a crisis
sections.body:
The S&P 500, an index representing 500 of the largest U.S. companies, fell 0.77%. The Nasdaq Composite, which has a heavy technology weighting, declined 0.92%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average, a 30-company blue-chip index, lost 0.67%. Declining stocks outnumbered advancers by 3.55 to 1 on the New York Stock Exchange and by 2.56 to 1 on Nasdaq.

Other assets also fell: GLD, an exchange-traded fund that tracks gold, dropped 3.93%; CPER, an exchange-traded fund that tracks copper futures, lost 2.29%; and Bitcoin, the largest digital asset, traded near $83,100 this morning. The U.S. Dollar Index remained near a two-month high around 101.2.

In contrast, the VIX measures expected volatility embedded in S&P 500 options and is often called Wall Street’s fear gauge. It rose only to about 16.1. In other words, the selloff was broad, but markets are still pricing an interest-rate and valuation shock — not financial panic. That divergence matters: a VIX move above 20 alongside further credit deterioration would be a more serious signal.

sections.heading: 3. The new story is credit: AI financing is becoming more expensive
sections.body:
A credit spread is the extra yield a company pays over a government bond to compensate investors for risk. Reuters reported that spreads on U.S. high-yield bonds widened toward 300 basis points — nearly 3 percentage points — their widest level since April. Investment-grade spreads, which ended last week around 81 basis points, have also begun to widen.

The pressure matters especially for artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Reuters reported that large cloud companies have issued roughly $220 billion of bonds this year, and the amount could roughly double next year. Nvidia, the world’s largest artificial-intelligence chipmaker, is exploring the use of insurers to share the risk in loans to smaller cloud customers whose chips serve as collateral, according to the Financial Times. These structures are still being explored; they are not a finished product.

The fact is that credit spreads have risen and AI participants are searching for new ways to distribute risk. The interpretation is that the bottleneck is expanding from chips to capital: the question is not only whether a data center can be built, but at what financing cost and who retains the equipment’s residual-value risk. This is not a credit crisis, but credit is providing an earlier warning than equity indexes.

sections.heading: 4. Oil remains above $105 even as Gulf exports recover
sections.body:
Brent is the global benchmark for crude oil prices. It settled Monday at $105.28 a barrel, up 0.9%, and traded near $106.60 this morning. West Texas Intermediate, the main U.S. crude benchmark, settled at $92.60. Prices jumped by more than $4 intraday after President Trump rejected Iran’s proposal, but surrendered most of the gain when Qatar announced further mediation efforts.

At the same time, crude exports from major Middle Eastern producers recovered to about 12.8 million barrels a day in September, the highest level since the war began. The fact is that barrels are still leaving the region, while a Hormuz risk premium remains embedded in prices.

XLE is an exchange-traded fund holding the largest energy companies in the S&P 500. It rose just 0.11% to $62.10, far less than oil’s early surge. That divergence does not prove fundamental weakness in energy companies, but it shows investors are not automatically chasing every increase in crude prices.

sections.heading: 5. Australia raised rates — another sign that monetary tightening is becoming global
sections.body:
The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 0.25 percentage point this morning to 4.60%, the highest level since 2011 and its fourth increase this year. The move was widely expected, but it came with Australia’s unemployment rate at 4.6%, a five-year high, and underlying inflation still near 3.6%.

Australia does not determine the direction of U.S. Treasury yields. It does reinforce the broader picture: higher energy prices and resilient demand are forcing central banks to prioritize inflation even as labor markets begin to soften. For long-term bond investors, that is a global headwind rather than only a U.S. story.

sections.heading: 6. Watchlist: what changed and what must happen next
sections.body:
• Forgent Power Solutions (FPS) makes transformers and power-distribution equipment for data centers and the grid. Its shares fell 6.15% to $36.59 and broke the $37 area we identified as support. No new company release or evidence directly linking the decline to Texas policy was found; the thesis stabilizes if FPS recovers above $38 and stops underperforming comparable electrical-equipment companies.
• Fluence Energy (FLNC) supplies utility-scale energy-storage systems. It fell 4.33% to $7.50; the execution warning remains in place until production and backlog conversion demonstrably improve.
• URNM is an exchange-traded fund holding uranium miners and nuclear-fuel companies. It fell 2.56% to $47.92; no new fundamental catalyst was found, so the move currently appears to be part of broad macro pressure.

title: Oil Is Back Near $107 — and Long-Term Yields Are Rising Again
summary:

What the market may be missing: stocks are not collapsing alongside bonds. What to watch today: whether Brent breaks above $108 and whether the 30-year yield remains above 5.50% after Wall Street opens. If both conditions hold and the long-term Treasury fund falls below $79, the bearish weekend scenario will receive further confirmation.

The evidence-supported explanation is that Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. At the same time, he said he expects talks to continue this week and that more than 20 million barrels passed through the strait over the weekend. Iran, for its part, has not signaled a willingness to soften its terms.

The fact is that oil rose and the current proposal was rejected. The interpretation is that the market restored part of the risk premium, but is not pricing a complete supply stoppage: Brent remains below the $108 threshold we identified yesterday. The claim about Hormuz traffic comes from Trump and is not a substitute for verified shipping data.

sections.heading: 2. The bond market confirmed part of the weekend’s bearish scenario
sections.body:
TLT is an iShares exchange-traded fund that holds U.S. Treasury bonds with maturities of 20 years or more, making its price especially sensitive to increases in long-term yields. It closed Friday at $79.32 and fell about 0.28% in overnight trading.

sections.heading: 3. Stocks are holding up better than bonds — because of the same strong economy
sections.body:

The divergence matters: government bonds respond to interest rates and inflation, while stocks also receive support from expectations for profit growth. Strong economic data can therefore push bond prices down without immediately causing a sharp equity decline.

It is a fact that the futures reaction is modest relative to the rise in yields. The hypothesis is that investors still believe growth and earnings can absorb higher financing costs. That hypothesis weakens if the decline broadens beyond technology and equity indexes lose Friday’s gains.

sections.body:
Gold fell this morning to about $4,262 an ounce, while copper declined to roughly $6.60 a pound after weak data from China. The U.S. Dollar Index rose to about 101.39, a two-month high.

That behavior separates two stories. Oil is rising because of a specific Middle East supply risk. Gold is under pressure from higher yields and a stronger dollar, while copper is also responding to concerns about Chinese demand.

The investor implication is that there is no confirmation yet of broad inflation across commodities. The immediate pressure is concentrated in energy and interest rates. A change in the picture would require copper and gold to rise alongside oil, rather than oil moving alone.

sections.heading: 1. The main story: long-term bonds keep breaking down
sections.body: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose yesterday to about 5.16%, while the 30-year yield climbed to about 5.45% — its highest level since 2004. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so the rise in yields reflects another decline in long-term bond prices. The trigger was a combination of stronger-than-expected business activity and a sharp rise in input prices, reviving concern that inflation will remain high. Investors increased their bets on another rate hike. On September 16, the Fed raised rates by 0.25 percentage point to a range of 3.75%–4.00% and said economic activity continued to expand at a solid pace while inflation remained elevated.

sections.heading: 2. And what does this mean for TLT?
sections.body: TLT is an iShares exchange-traded fund that holds U.S. Treasury bonds with maturities longer than 20 years, making it especially sensitive to changes in long-term yields. When the 30-year yield rises quickly, the fund's price tends to fall. The current area may look cheaper to a long-term investor, but cheap does not mean the bottom is already in. The positive thesis strengthens if the 10-year yield returns below 5% and the 30-year yield falls from the 5.4%–5.45% area; it weakens if yields remain at these levels or continue to rise.

sections.heading: 3. Oil has again become a macro variable
sections.body: Oil is not only a story about energy companies. When it remains at elevated levels, it affects transportation and production costs and inflation expectations — and therefore interest rates and bond yields. Diplomatic progress with Iran could reduce the risk premium and ease inflation somewhat; by contrast, failed talks or another supply disruption could bring the pressure back. That is why, in my view, oil and the 10- and 30-year yields are currently the same macro story viewed from different angles.

sections.heading: 4. Energy stocks are still holding up
sections.body: XLE is an exchange-traded fund that groups the largest energy companies in the S&P 500, led by ExxonMobil and Chevron. Yesterday it closed at $62.60, up 0.37%, while the broader stock market barely advanced. But an important point is that the fund has already benefited greatly from the rise in energy. I therefore would not automatically interpret every further increase in oil as a new opportunity; investors need to examine how much of the scenario is already reflected in company prices.

sections.heading: 5. U.S.–China: a ceasefire, not a peace agreement
sections.body:
The Trump–Xi meeting ended without a major breakthrough. The clearest economic development was an extension of the trade truce by only two months.
The major issues — tariffs, Chinese purchases, rare earths and technology restrictions — remained open. This is short-term relief, but not a structural change in U.S.–China relations.
For semiconductors and AI, the main implication is that no new tightening of restrictions was created for now, but access for U.S. companies to the Chinese market was not meaningfully reopened either.

sections.heading: 6. What the market may be missing: stocks are not breaking with bonds
sections.body:
This is, in my view, the most interesting picture this morning.
On one side:
10Y above 5% → 30Y around 5.4%–5.45% → Brent oil around $100+ → the Fed has already raised rates.
On the other side, the S&P 500 ended yesterday almost unchanged after recovering from its intraday low. This is a divergence — a mismatch between markets.
One possibility: the stock market is right, and the economy and earnings are strong enough to cope with interest rates.
A second possibility: the bond market is repricing the cost of capital faster than the stock market.
This is exactly the gap I want to track.

sections.heading: 7. Bitcoin: a positive data point beneath the surface
sections.body: IBIT is BlackRock's exchange-traded fund that tracks the price of Bitcoin. On September 24, U.S. Bitcoin funds recorded net inflows of about $191 million, led by roughly $163 million into IBIT. The figure is positive for institutional demand even if Bitcoin's price does not immediately break higher. Still, one day of flows is not enough to prove a trend change, so the key is whether the streak continues alongside price stability.

sections.heading: 8. AI and electricity: the bottleneck remains physical
sections.body: The data-center power-infrastructure story continues to receive further confirmation. Accelevation, a company that designs and manufactures power distribution, cooling and modular infrastructure for data centers, is targeting a valuation of up to $5.37 billion in its IPO. This reinforces the argument that the market is beginning to distinguish between “AI” as software and the physical equipment that makes the computing possible. Forgent Power Solutions (FPS) makes electrical distribution equipment for data centers and the power grid, so it is relevant to the same bottleneck. No new reliable fundamental report on FPS itself was found this morning, so there is no reason to attribute a catalyst to the stock that does not exist.

sections.heading: 9. Copper and metals
sections.body: There is an interesting long-term monitoring point here: Reuters argues that higher energy prices could accelerate the shift to electric vehicles in parts of the world, while also increasing future pressure on copper, lithium and nickel supply chains if mining investment fails to keep pace with demand. This is not a catalyst for today's trading, but it reinforces why copper remains on our list of strategic themes.

marketMap: Market map: strong activity and higher input prices → expectations for more Fed tightening → the 10-year yield above 5% and the 30-year around 5.45% → pressure on TLT and growth-stock multiples. At the same time, high oil strengthens inflation risk. Contrarian check: the consensus is that long-term bonds remain risky and there is no reason to rush into duration. It may be wrong if progress with Iran lowers oil, inflation data weaken and yields above 5% attract new demand. This thesis breaks if the 30-year yield remains above 5.4% while oil and inflation stay sticky.
calendar:
Catalyst Calendar — Over the next 24 hours: oil and possible progress with Iran; the reaction of the 10- and 30-year yields after the sharp rise. September 30: August PCE data, the third estimate of second-quarter GDP and the BEA annual data update; Micron is also expected to report that day, with market expectations of about $50.8 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $31.43 per share. Further ahead: the next Fed decision is scheduled for October 27–28.
Watchlist — TLT: whether long-term yields begin to fall. XLE: whether relative strength holds without another oil surge. FPS: no new report; watch performance versus other electrical-infrastructure companies. MU: earnings on September 30. IBIT/Bitcoin: whether fund inflows continue.
takeaway: Bottom line: the 30-year U.S. Treasury yield is at its highest level since 2004, but the stock market is still refusing to break with it. That gap can close through lower yields — or through a delayed adjustment in equities. For now, oil, long-term yields and the reaction of growth stocks are the three variables to monitor. This is market news and monitoring, not personalized advice.

title: Morning Brief · The Economy Is Too Strong for TLT — and Yields Are Back Above 5%
summary:
What changed: U.S. activity data were much stronger than expected. The services PMI rose to 58.7 versus a 56.0 consensus, the 10-year Treasury yield jumped about 16 basis points to roughly 5.12%, and TLT fell 1.54% to $80.46.
What the market may be missing: this was not merely a response to higher oil. The 10-year real yield also rose sharply, while demand at the five-year Treasury auction was weak. Investors are demanding higher yields because of both inflation risk and debt supply.
What to watch today: the seven-year Treasury auction and TLT's ability to hold above $80. A lower-than-expected jobless-claims reading or another weak auction could keep the 10-year yield above 5%; a well-received auction could provide relief.

sections.heading: 1. Activity data reversed the TLT story in a single day
sections.body: S&P Global's U.S. Composite PMI rose to 58.4 in September from 56.0, the fastest pace in more than five years. The services index reached 58.7 versus a 56.0 consensus and 56.5 in August, while manufacturing jumped to 57.0 versus a 53.6 consensus and 53.9 previously. Price pressures also intensified. The fact: growth and prices were stronger than expected. The market reaction: the 10-year yield rose about 16 basis points to roughly 5.12%, the 30-year yield reached about 5.41%, and TLT fell 1.54% to $80.46. The investor implication: lower oil alone is not enough when domestic activity reinforces the case for higher interest rates.

sections.heading: 2. TLT's decline went beyond inflation fears
sections.body: Yesterday we were looking for TLT to break above $82.18; instead, the fund fell as low as $80.23 and closed at $80.46. The two-year yield is near 4.90%, the 10-year around 5.12% and the 30-year around 5.41%. The 10-year TIPS yield, a rough measure of the return after stripping out expected inflation, also rose to about 2.79%. The Treasury selloff therefore did not reflect inflation expectations alone: the real return investors demand also increased. The TLT thesis will begin to improve only if the 10-year yield falls back below 5% and the fund reclaims $81.50; a break below $80 would reopen the risk of new lows.

sections.heading: 3. The undercovered issue: demand for government debt also weakened
sections.body: Alongside the strong macro data, the Treasury's $70 billion five-year auction cleared at a higher yield than the market level immediately before the sale. In plain terms, the Treasury had to offer a higher return to attract buyers. This matters for TLT because even if inflation eases, heavy bond supply and demand that fails to keep pace can leave long-term yields elevated. A seven-year Treasury auction is scheduled for today. Strong demand would be reassuring; another weak result would support the view that the pressure is coming from government financing needs as well as the Fed.

sections.heading: 4. Stocks, gold and Bitcoin fell together — this looks like a rate shock
sections.body: SPY fell 0.74%, QQQ lost 0.84% and DIA declined 0.72%. Assets that sometimes serve as inflation hedges also weakened: GLD fell 1.82%, CPER dropped 1.96% and Bitcoin traded near $83,900, down about 3.8%. Micron lost 2.20% after Tuesday's sharp gain. When equities, long-duration bonds, gold, copper and crypto all fall together, the most consistent explanation is a rise in the price of money — higher yields — rather than a separate negative event in every asset. The dollar strengthened to around a two-month high, adding pressure on commodities.

sections.heading: 5. Oil is back above $102, making the bond problem harder
sections.body: After falling below $100, Brent traded this morning near $102.30 and WTI around $91.50. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has restarted, but only at a partial rate, while uncertainty surrounding U.S.-Iran talks continues to leave supply risk in the market. The pipeline is operating; oil nevertheless failed to remain below $100. For TLT, the combination of strong economic activity and rebounding oil is more difficult than either factor alone. XLE rose 0.97% to $62.37 but remains below its levels from the start of the week.

sections.heading: 6. FPS continues to outperform its peer group
sections.body: FPS gained 3.50% to $39.88 and closed near its session high, even as Vertiv fell 1.83% and Eaton lost 0.85%; Powell Industries gained 0.26%. This is the second session in which FPS has not behaved as though the Texas decision created an immediate, company-specific hit. However, no new fundamental announcement was found to explain the gain, so it is too early to attribute the move to an improvement in the business. The positive signal strengthens if FPS holds above $39–$40 as volume normalizes; it weakens if the stock falls below $37 or begins to lag its peers consistently.

sections.heading: 7. Watchlist: what changed and what did not
sections.body: TLT: fell to $80.46; the immediate test is $80 below and $81.50 above. FPS: rose to $39.88 and continues to show relative resilience, with no newly verified catalyst. Fluence gained 4.33% to $7.58, but its production and execution warning has not changed. URNM fell 4.11% to $50.62; no new fundamental event was found that independently explains the decline. BHF finished nearly unchanged at $51.99 with no verified transaction update. TIGR fell 3.69% to $4.71, while JEPQ slipped 0.14% to $61.10. No new fundamental catalyst in energy storage or copper justified changing the thesis beyond the broad yield shock.

marketMap: Market map: strong activity data and rising price pressures → the market raises the probability of another Fed hike → the 10-year yield returns to about 5.12% and the 30-year to roughly 5.41% → TLT falls and equity multiples come under pressure. At the same time, a weak Treasury auction shows that the pressure is not coming only from the Fed, but also from the need to find buyers for heavy debt supply. The simultaneous declines in equities, gold, copper and Bitcoin reinforce the conclusion that this was primarily a broad yield shock.
calendar:
Over the next 24 hours: U.S. weekly jobless claims; the U.S. Treasury's seven-year note auction; the Trump-Xi summit, with markets focused on trade, semiconductors, AI, Taiwan and Iran; and pricing of SoftBank's more than $11 billion bond sale to fund its OpenAI investment.
Over the next seven days: Xi's U.S. visit concludes Friday; on September 30, markets expect August PCE data, the third estimate of second-quarter GDP and the BEA annual data update.
Further ahead: the next Fed decision is scheduled for October 28.
takeaway: Contrarian check: the consensus after the activity data is that the economy is too strong and the Fed will need to raise rates again, so yields and TLT will continue in yesterday's direction. That may be right if jobless claims remain low, the seven-year auction is weak and the 10-year yield holds above 5.10%. It may be wrong because a 16-basis-point one-day jump already prices in much of the surprise, while yields above 5% could attract new buyers. The bearish TLT thesis weakens if the seven-year auction is strong, the 10-year yield falls below 5% and TLT reclaims $81.50. It strengthens if TLT breaks below $80 and the 30-year yield holds above 5.40%. This is market news and monitoring, not personalized advice.

title: Morning Brief · Oil Surges, Technology Weakens and the Fed Faces a Test
summary: September 14, 2026: Brent returned to roughly $108 after the Oman meeting on the Strait of Hormuz was postponed and the Saudi pipeline remained closed. Calls to slow AI development also drove sharp declines in Asian chip stocks and Nasdaq futures. The week opens with two distinct pressure points: energy and rates, and a new AI-valuation risk.

sections.heading: 1. Oil: the weekend scenario begins to materialize
sections.body: Brent rose about 3.1% this morning to $107.82 per barrel and WTI gained roughly 3.2% to $103.22. The Oman meeting planned for today between Iran and Gulf states was postponed, while Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline remained closed following the drone attack. Sources cited by Reuters said inventories at Yanbu could cover roughly five to seven days of exports; if the pipeline does not resume operation, as much as 4% of global supply could be at risk. The market mechanism is clear: fewer available export routes, higher shipping and insurance costs and a larger risk premium in crude prices.

sections.heading: 2. Futures point to a split opening
sections.body: In early trading, S&P 500 futures were down about 0.35% and Nasdaq 100 futures around 1.1%, while Dow futures were near flat. The gap suggests this is not merely an oil reaction: technology is also dealing with a separate AI event. Energy and defensive sectors may hold up better, while semiconductors, software, airlines, transport and energy-intensive industries are more sensitive. These are early futures and may change before the 4:30 p.m. Israel-time open.

sections.heading: 3. AI and chip stocks: a new risk factor beyond rates
sections.body: AI-related shares fell sharply in Asia after leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI supported slowing model development for safety reasons. SoftBank fell as much as 13.2%, Kioxia 9.8%, SK Hynix 5.3%, Samsung Electronics 3.7% and TSMC 1.2%. For U.S. investors, possible pressure on Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and the data-center supply chain now reflects not only higher yields but also concern that AI investment and regulation could change. It is too early to infer a fundamental shift in demand, but the technology story itself is now competing with oil as a market driver.

sections.heading: 4. TLT: little cushion before the 5% test
sections.body: The U.S. 10-year yield traded near 4.97% this morning and the 30-year around 5.37%. TLT ended Friday at $80.87; according to iShares, its 30-day SEC yield was 5.29% and effective duration 14.97 years. As a rough approximation, a 10-basis-point increase in yields could reduce the fund’s price by about 1.5% before convexity and curve effects. A move in the 30-year yield from 5.37% to 5.50% could therefore add roughly 2% pressure to TLT, though this is not a precise price forecast. Today’s key test is whether the 10-year breaks 5% and the 30-year settles above 5.40%.

sections.heading: 5. The Fed: the decision looks expected, the message less so
sections.body: Rate futures implied an approximately 86% probability of a 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday—the first increase since mid-2023. Markets also priced roughly 90 basis points of tightening through the second half of 2027. A surprise decision to hold could push long yields higher if seen as insufficient resolve against inflation. Conversely, a hike presented as a one-off move could ease yields and offer TLT relief. The dollar index rose to 99.22, while the yen remained near a seven-month high ahead of the Bank of Japan decision.

sections.heading: 6. Watch themes: energy, uranium, storage and copper
sections.body: XLE finished Friday at $65.14 and may benefit from higher oil, but the better signal will be whether it approaches its 52-week high rather than lagging crude. URNM fell 4.06%; no new fundamental report has invalidated the nuclear-demand thesis, so the question is whether weakness persists while energy prices rise. There is no material new copper development versus the previous brief. In energy storage, no new contract or project justifies action; expensive oil does not automatically translate into BESS profits, while higher rates increase financing costs for capital-intensive projects.

marketMap: Morning market map: pipeline closure and postponed talks → Brent near $108 → inflation pressure and stronger tightening expectations → the 10-year near 5% and the 30-year around 5.37% → pressure on TLT and growth multiples. A second chain is also active: calls to slow AI → declines in Asian chip shares → Nasdaq futures underperform. A partial pipeline restart, a new date for talks, or a market response in which oil stays high while yields and the Nasdaq stop falling could reverse the picture.

takeaway: No single trade explains everything today. Oil raises inflation risk while AI faces an independent risk event. For TLT, the test is whether the 10-year crosses 5% and the 30-year settles above 5.40%. Contrarian check: if yields fail to break higher and the Nasdaq pares losses despite Brent near $108 and weakness in Asia, markets may already have absorbed much of the negative news. title: Morning Brief · Weekend Developments Put Oil and the Fed Back at the Center
summary: September 13, 2026: Wall Street ended Friday higher and oil retreated from its peaks, but weekend developments in the Strait of Hormuz and at the Saudi oil pipeline renewed supply risk. Ahead of the new week, the decisive chain is oil, inflation and yields, culminating in Wednesday’s Fed decision.

sections.heading: 1. Weekend news: supply risk rises again
sections.body: Reuters reported this morning that UKMTO had received a report of a projectile striking a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Saudi Arabia temporarily closed the East–West pipeline after a drone attack. In recent months the pipeline had carried roughly four to five million barrels per day—about 4%–5% of global supply—and served as a major bypass while passage through Hormuz was restricted. These events occurred after Friday’s Wall Street close and were therefore not fully reflected in closing prices. A possible implication for the week’s open is a renewed oil risk premium, relative support for energy and renewed pressure on bonds and rate-sensitive equities.

sections.heading: 2. Friday was positive, but the week remained negative
sections.body: On Friday, the S&P 500 gained 0.86%, the Nasdaq 0.96% and the Dow Jones 0.98% after four consecutive declining sessions. For the week, however, the S&P 500 lost 0.8%, the Nasdaq fell 0.7% and the Dow declined 1.6%. The daily rebound was supported by oil retreating from its highs and a slight easing at the long end of the Treasury market. Brent settled at $104.61 and WTI at $100.05, although both still gained more than 8% for the week. Friday’s close therefore looked more like temporary relief than a confirmed change in trend.

sections.heading: 3. Headline inflation matched expectations, but energy keeps filtering through
sections.body: The U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in August and 3.4% year over year. Core CPI increased 0.3% for the month and 2.4% over the year. Within the report, gasoline rose 3.9% for the month and energy overall gained 2.1%; over 12 months, energy was up 16.3%. The headline figure matched the forecast, but monthly core inflation exceeded the 0.2% consensus reported in market surveys. By Friday’s close, rate futures implied an approximately 87%–90% probability of a 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday. The more important question is no longer only whether the Fed will raise rates, but whether it presents the move as a one-off adjustment or the start of another tightening cycle.

sections.heading: 4. TLT and long Treasuries: an extreme zone, not a guaranteed bottom
sections.body: TLT closed Friday at $80.87, up just 0.11%, after an intraday low of $80.61. The U.S. 10-year yield ended near 4.96% and the 30-year around 5.35%–5.36%; during the week, the 30-year touched roughly 5.38%, its highest level since 2007. This is an area where TLT’s long-term risk-reward becomes more interesting, but weekend news could reactivate the oil–inflation–yields chain and produce further price weakness. A practical conclusion is to watch the 30-year yield around 5.35%–5.50% rather than treating a historically low fund price as proof that the bottom is in.

sections.heading: 5. Energy, uranium and metals
sections.body: XLE rose 0.35% on Friday to $65.14 even as oil fell nearly 3%, a relative-strength signal worth watching if crude opens higher again. URNM, by contrast, fell 4.06% to $52.38, while its official NAV declined 3.68%. No new verified fundamental event was found that could independently explain the drop, so it is more accurate for now to view it as sharp profit-taking in the miners basket rather than inventing a cause. Copper closed near $6.47 per pound, still close to recent highs, and gold recovered Friday to $4,363 per ounce despite higher rate expectations. The cross-asset message is mixed: markets are paying for scarcity and fiscal risk while punishing yield-sensitive assets as long-term rates rise.

sections.heading: 6. Securities on the watchlist
sections.body: BHF fell 1.40% on Friday to $50.11, with no newly verified transaction update. Against the stated $70 deal price, an unusually wide gap of roughly 39.7% remained, indicating that the market was still pricing completion and timing risk. TIGR declined 1.43% to $4.83, while JEPQ gained 0.79% to $59.78. In energy storage, there was no sufficiently material new public catalyst to turn the theme into a trade idea that morning. It remained on the radar because of the structural relationship between AI loads, grid-connection constraints and backup-power demand.

marketMap: Market map for the week’s open: escalation in Hormuz and on the Saudi route → higher oil and risk premium → stronger inflation and rate-hike expectations → higher long-term yields → pressure on TLT and growth multiples. What could reverse the chain: a rapid pipeline restart, a breakthrough at Monday’s Oman meeting between Gulf states and Iran, or an oil price that fails to rise despite the news. Contrarian check: if oil opens higher but Treasury yields do not rise and TLT holds above its low, the market may already be saturated with fear and part of the negative scenario may already be priced in.

title: Evening Update · Inflation and Energy Take Center Stage
summary: September 10, 2026: U.S. producer prices rose in August, higher Treasury yields weighed on equities, and attention turned to the Consumer Price Index and the Federal Reserve meeting. This is an intraday snapshot published before the Wall Street close.

sections.heading: 1. Producer prices: energy stands out
sections.body:
According to the BLS, the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.4% in August and 5.4% over the year. Excluding food, energy and trade services, the index increased 0.3% for the month and 4.7% year over year.
The energy component jumped 4.2%, while diesel fuel prices rose 24.1%. These are monthly changes in producer prices, not the daily move in crude oil.
The implication: producer-price pressure may eventually reach consumers, but pass-through is not automatic; corporate margins and demand also affect it.

sections.heading: 2. Wall Street: yields rise and equities weaken
sections.body:
Reuters reported intraday declines in U.S. equities alongside higher Treasury yields and oil prices and renewed concern about inflation. These were interim figures, not closing data.
Interpretation: higher yields intensify competition for investor capital and can weigh on growth-stock valuations. More expensive energy may support oil producers while raising costs for transport and industrial companies.

sections.heading: 3. American Eagle: the outlook outweighs the revenue beat
sections.body:
According to Reuters, American Eagle shares fell roughly 11% intraday after the company guided to no improvement in gross margin in the following quarter and reported weakness in its core brand, despite revenue exceeding expectations.
The lesson: a stock’s response to earnings depends on guidance and prospective profitability as well as reported revenue. One company’s results are not enough to draw conclusions about the consumer as a whole.

marketMap: The central chain this evening is energy → inflation → Treasury yields → equity valuations. This is an analytical framework, not a forecast: lower energy prices or a softer inflation reading could change the picture. It is important to distinguish broad-market moves from company-specific news.

September 15–16: Federal Reserve meeting, including economic projections, according to the Federal Reserve calendar.
These dates and times refer to scheduled releases, not results that have already been published.
takeaway: The producer-price report points to price pressure, particularly in energy. Tomorrow’s CPI will be the next key checkpoint ahead of the Fed. This is market news and monitoring; each reader makes their own decisions.
